# Legend: Shape Size and Alpha {#ggplot2-legend-shape-size-alpha}

In this chapter, we modify legends when shape, size or alpha is mapped to variables.

:::{.callout-note}
## Why this matters

Shape, size and alpha encode extra variables without new panels; map size and alpha to continuous variables only.
:::

:::{.callout-warning}
## Common pitfall

Mapping size or alpha to a discrete variable produces a misleading legend.
:::

```{r setup-legend-cf, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, results='hide', message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
```

## How to change legend point shapes in ggplot2 {#change-legend-point-shapes}

We will learn to modify the following using `scale_shape_manual` when `shape` is mapped to categorical variables:

- title
- breaks
- limits
- labels
- values

### How to create a plot with a shape legend in ggplot2 {#plot .unnumbered}

Let us start with a scatter plot examining the relationship between displacement
and miles per gallon from the mtcars data set. We will map the shape of the points
to the `cyl` variable. 

```{r legs16, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, shape = factor(cyl)))
```

As you can see, the legend acts as a guide for the `shape` aesthetic. Now, let 
us learn to modify the different aspects of the legend.

### How to change the shape legend title in ggplot2 {#shape-legend-title .unnumbered}

The title of the legend (`factor(cyl)`) is not very intuitive. If the user does 
not know the underlying data, they will not make any sense of it. 
Let us change it to `Cylinders` using the `name` argument.

```{r legs17, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, shape = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_shape_manual(name = "Cylinders", values = c(4, 12, 24))
```

If you have mapped shape or size to a discrete variable with fewer than six
categories, you can use `scale_shape()`.

```{r legs18, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, shape = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_shape(name = 'Cylinders')
```

### How to change legend shape values in ggplot2 {#shape-legend-values .unnumbered}

To change the default shapes in the legend, use the `values` argument and
supply a numeric vector of shapes. The number of shapes must equal
the number of levels in the categorical variable mapped.
In the example below, `cyl` has 3 levels (4, 6, 8) and hence we have specified
3 different shapes.

```{r legs19, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, shape = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(4, 12, 24))
```

### How to change shape legend labels in ggplot2 {#shape-legend-labels .unnumbered}

We can modify the labels in the legend using the `labels` argument. Let us 
change the labels to `Four`, `Six` and `Eight` in the next example. Ensure that
the labels are intuitive and easy to interpret for the end user of the plot.

```{r legs20, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, shape = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(4, 12, 24), labels = c('Four', 'Six', 'Eight'))
```

### How to change shape legend limits in ggplot2 {#shape-legend-limits .unnumbered}

Let us assume that we want to modify the data to be displayed: instead of 
examining the relationship between mileage and displacement for all cars, we 
want to look at only cars with at least 6 cylinders. One way to do this
is to filter the data using `filter` from dplyr and then visualize it. 
Instead, we will use the `limits` argument and filter the data for visualization.


```{r legs21, fig.align='center'}
#| warning: true
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, shape = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("4" = 4, "6" = 12, "8" = 24),
    limits = c("6", "8"))
```

Unlike color, `shape` cannot draw an out-of-range group in grey: the
four-cylinder cars are removed before plotting, and ggplot2 reports the number
of rows it removed. The legend shows only 6 and 8 cylinders. Filter the data
with `filter()` if you want to remove them yourself.

### How to reorder or hide shape legend items in ggplot2 {#shape-legend-breaks .unnumbered}

When there are a large number of levels in the mapped variable, you may not 
want the labels in the legend to represent all of them. In such cases, we can 
use the breaks argument and specify which levels to show in the legend. In the
example below, we use the `breaks` argument to ensure that the labels in the
legend represent two levels (4, 8) of the mapped variable.

```{r legs22, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, shape = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("4" = 4, "6" = 12, "8" = 24),
    breaks = c("4", "8"))
```

`breaks` hides the 6-cylinder key but keeps every point: the six-cylinder cars
still use shape 12. With unnamed values, the shapes are matched to `breaks` and
the unlisted group is removed instead.

### How to combine shape legend options in ggplot2 {#putting-it-all-together .unnumbered}

```{r legs23, fig.align='center'}
#| warning: true
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, shape = factor(cyl))) +
  scale_shape_manual(name = "Cylinders", labels = c('Six', 'Eight'),
    values = c("6" = 12, "8" = 24), limits = c("6", "8"),
    breaks = c("6", "8"))
```

The four-cylinder cars are outside the limits, so ggplot2 removes them and
reports it. The legend lists only the two remaining groups.

## How to change legend point sizes in ggplot2 {#change-legend-point-sizes}

We will learn to modify the following using `scale_size_continuous` when the `size` aesthetic is mapped to variables:

- title
- breaks
- limits
- range
- labels
- values

### How to create a plot with a size legend in ggplot2 {#plot-1 .unnumbered}

Let us start with a scatter plot examining the relationship between displacement
and miles per gallon from the mtcars data set. We will map the size of the points
to the `hp` variable. Remember, `size` must always be mapped to a continuous 
variable.

```{r legs24}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, size = hp))
```

As you can see, the legend acts as a guide for the `size` aesthetic. Now, let 
us learn to modify the different aspects of the legend.

### How to change the size legend title in ggplot2 {#size-legend-title .unnumbered}

The title of the legend (`hp`) is not very intuitive. If the user does 
not know the underlying data, they will not make any sense of it. 
Let us change it to `Horsepower` using the `name` argument.

```{r legs25}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, size = hp)) +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Horsepower")
```

### How to change the legend size range in ggplot2 {#size-legend-range .unnumbered}

We can modify the range of the size of points using the `range` argument. We
need to specify a lower and upper range using a numeric vector. In the example
below, we use `range` and supply the lower and upper limits as `3` and `6`. 
The size of the points now lies between `3` and `6` only.

```{r legs26}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, size = hp)) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(3, 6))
```

### How to change size legend limits in ggplot2 {#size-legend-limits .unnumbered}

Let us assume that we want to modify the data to be displayed: instead of 
examining the relationship between mileage and displacement for all cars, we 
want to look at only cars whose horsepower is between `100` and `350`. 
One way to do this is to filter the data using `filter` from dplyr 
and then visualize it. Instead, we will use the `limits` argument and filter 
the data for visualization.

```{r legs27}
#| warning: true
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, size = hp)) +
  scale_size_continuous(limits = c(100, 350))
```

`limits` removes the rows whose horsepower is outside 100--350, so the plot and
the legend only describe the remaining cars; ggplot2 warns that it removed
them.

### How to reorder or hide size legend items in ggplot2 {#size-legend-breaks .unnumbered}

When the range of the variable mapped to size is large, you may not 
want the labels in the legend to represent all of them. In such cases, we can 
use the breaks argument and specify the labels to be used. In the example
below, we use the `breaks` argument to ensure that the labels in the legend
represent certain midpoints (125, 200, 275) of the mapped variable.

```{r legs28}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, size = hp)) +
  scale_size_continuous(breaks = c(125, 200, 275))
```

### How to change size legend labels in ggplot2 {#size-legend-labels .unnumbered}

We can modify the labels in the legend using the `labels` argument. Let us 
change the labels to "1 Hundred", "2 Hundred" and "3 Hundred" in the next example. 
Ensure that the labels are intuitive and easy to interpret for the end user of 
the plot.

```{r legs29}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, size = hp)) +
  scale_size_continuous(breaks = c(100, 200, 300),
    labels = c("1 Hundred", "2 Hundred", "3 Hundred"))
```

### How to combine size legend options in ggplot2 {#putting-it-all-together-1 .unnumbered}

```{r legs30}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, size = hp)) +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Horsepower", range = c(3, 6), 
    limits = c(0, 400), breaks = c(100, 200, 300),
    labels = c("1 Hundred", "2 Hundred", "3 Hundred"))
```

## How to change legend transparency in ggplot2 {#change-legend-transparency}

We will learn to modify the following using `scale_alpha_continuous()` when `alpha` or transparency is mapped to variables:

- title
- breaks
- limits
- range
- labels
- values

### How to create a plot with an alpha legend in ggplot2 {#plot-2 .unnumbered}

Let us start with a scatter plot examining the relationship between displacement
and miles per gallon from the mtcars data set. We will map the transparency of 
the points to the `hp` variable. Remember, `alpha` must always be mapped to a 
continuous variable.

```{r legs31, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, alpha = hp), color = 'blue')
```

As you can see, the legend acts as a guide for the `alpha` aesthetic. Now, let 
us learn to modify the different aspects of the legend.

### How to change the transparency legend title in ggplot2 {#alpha-legend-title .unnumbered}

The title of the legend (`hp`) is not very intuitive. If the user does 
not know the underlying data, they will not make any sense of it. 
Let us change it to `Horsepower` using the `name` argument.

```{r legs32, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, alpha = hp), color = 'blue') +
  scale_alpha_continuous("Horsepower")
```

### How to reorder or hide alpha legend items in ggplot2 {#alpha-legend-breaks .unnumbered}

When the range of the variable mapped to alpha is large, you may not 
want the labels in the legend to represent all of them. In such cases, we can 
use the breaks argument and specify the labels to be used. In the example
below, we use the `breaks` argument to ensure that the labels in the legend
represent certain midpoints (125, 200, 275) of the mapped variable.

```{r legs33, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, alpha = hp), color = 'blue') +
  scale_alpha_continuous(breaks = c(125, 200, 275))
```

### How to change transparency legend limits in ggplot2 {#alpha-legend-limits .unnumbered}

Let us assume that we want to change the range shown in the legend: instead of
the full range of horsepower, we want the legend to cover only cars whose
horsepower is between `100` and `350`. One way to do this is to filter the data
using `filter` from dplyr and then visualize it. Instead, we will use the
`limits` argument to set the legend range; the data itself is not filtered.

```{r legs34, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, alpha = hp), color = 'blue') +
  scale_alpha_continuous(limits = c(100, 350))
```

Points outside the limits get `alpha = NA`, which ggplot2 draws fully opaque,
so the nine cars with horsepower below `100` stay on the plot and no warning is
raised.

### How to change the legend transparency range in ggplot2 {#alpha-legend-range .unnumbered}

We can modify the range of the transparency of points using the `range` 
argument. We need to specify a lower and upper range using a numeric vector. 
In the example below, we use `range` and supply the lower and upper limits as 
`0.4` and `0.8`. The transparency of the points now lies between `0.4` and 
`0.8` only.

```{r legs35, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, alpha = hp), color = 'blue') +
  scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.4, 0.8))
```

### How to change transparency legend labels in ggplot2 {#alpha-legend-labels .unnumbered}

We can modify the labels in the legend using the `labels` argument. Let us 
change the labels to "1 Hundred", "2 Hundred" and "3 Hundred" in the next example. 
Ensure that the labels are intuitive and easy to interpret for the end user of 
the plot.

```{r legs36, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, alpha = hp), color = 'blue') +
  scale_alpha_continuous(breaks = c(100, 200, 300),
    labels = c("1 Hundred", "2 Hundred", 
      "3 Hundred"))
```

### How to combine transparency legend options in ggplot2 {#putting-it-all-together-2 .unnumbered}

```{r legs37, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, alpha = hp), color = 'blue') +
  scale_alpha_continuous("Horsepower", breaks = c(100, 200, 300),
    limits = c(100, 350), range = c(0.4, 0.8),
    labels = c("1 Hundred", "2 Hundred", "3 Hundred"))
```


## Exercises

1. Map `shape` to cylinders with `scale_shape_manual(values = ...)`.
2. Control point spread with `scale_size_continuous(range = ...)`.
3. Explain why `size`/`alpha` must map to continuous variables.
